stories.title: Intel suffers worst stock drop in decades on weak forecast
stories.summary: Intel Corp suffered its worst stock rout in more than four decades after the PC industry slump and supply-chain snags hurt its forecast, renewing fears about the chipmaker’s turnaround bid.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Intel因疲弱预测遭遇数十年来最严重股价暴跌
stories.content:
(Oct 31): Intel Corp suffered its worst stock rout in more than four decades after the PC industry slump and supply-chain snags hurt its forecast, renewing fears about the chipmaker’s turnaround bid.

Sales in the fourth quarter will be US$15 billion (RM61 billion) to US$16 billion, the chipmaker said in a statement on Thursday. Analysts on average estimated US$17 billion, and some projections topped US$18 billion, according to data compiled by *Bloomberg*. Profit will be 25 cents a share in the quarter, excluding certain items. Wall Street was projecting adjusted earnings of 43 cents a share.

Intel is contending with a severe slump in the personal computer market. Makers of laptops and desktops — key customers — are struggling with shortages of memory semiconductors and surging component prices. That’s cut into PC shipments and hurt demand from users. In addition, chief executive officer Lip-Bu Tan said his company’s data centre unit would have done even better if it hadn’t suffered from shortages of some raw materials and a shutdown of a factory in Israel — supply snags that the company is working hard to fix.

“I am a bit disappointed in terms of how we cannot fulfil the customer requirements,” Tan said in an interview.

As to the PC market, “one of the main challenges, basically, is memory”, he said. “Memory pricing went up a lot. I think my prediction is that in 2027 it is going to be a very severe issue to all of us. We are not alone — it’s just the whole market is impacted.”

Intel’s stock fell 29% to US$65.76 at the close Friday in New York, marking its worst decline according to records dating back to 1982.

Intel projects the PC downturn will persist through at least the first half of 2027 — with a decline of 10% next year following a 12% slide in 2026. Still, longer term, the company is optimistic about demand for its products and is increasing its spending on new equipment to boost production. It’s growing more confident it will attract orders from other chipmakers that want to use its factories to build their components, Tan said.

Intel’s stock had more than doubled this year through Thursday’s close, with investors betting that the company will emerge as a key AI beneficiary. The increasing deployment of artificial intelligence services has created demand for Intel’s general-purpose chips, allowing it an entry into a market dominated by the technology of Nvidia Corp.

“Intel’s earnings highlight the challenges the company faces in pushing its recent turnaround into a sustained recovery,” Emarketer senior analyst Asa Hiken said in a note. Though demand for server processors is booming, “Intel’s disappointing outlook shows that strong demand alone isn’t enough to overcome its near-term challenges, particularly ongoing weakness in its traditional PC business,” he said.

Intel has been pursuing a turnaround under Tan, who took the helm in March 2025. He has improved the chipmaker’s finances, cut jobs and attracted major outside investors — including Nvidia and the US government. More recently, the company offered new stock to further support its comeback.

Intel still is working to restore its technological leadership, something that once made it the envy of Silicon Valley. The company also is seeking major customers for its chip foundry business, which manufactures components for outside clients. Without those customers in place, Intel is stuck with expensive facilities that only produce internal products.

Intel executives said they expect spending on new plants and equipment to be about US$20 billion in 2026 — and then increase significantly next year. On a conference call with analysts, chief financial officer Dave Zinsner described 2027 as an “investment year” for Intel as it tries to improve output to meet rising demand. That will be particularly true for data centre products, he said. The company will likely not generate free cash flow in that period, Zinsner said.

In the fourth quarter, the shutdown of a plant in Israel will cost US$300 million in lost revenue. The company is anticipating a similar shortfall in the first three months of next year, Zinsner said. The factory, which experienced a fire, has been closed for two weeks but will begin running again in the next few days. Chips take about three months to go from raw silicon to finished components. A power outage while silicon wafers are inside a machine often causes them to be scrapped.

Third-quarter sales rose 21% to US$16.5 billion, in line with analysts’ average estimate. Earnings were 52 cents a share in the period, which ended Sept 26. Analysts projected 41 cents.

Intel’s data centre and AI unit had revenue of US$7.3 billion, a gain of 78%. Sales in the client division, which makes chips for personal computers, declined 5% to US$8.1 billion.

The mixed picture shows the effect that the AI boom has had on Intel’s business. Though data centre infrastructure is fuelling demand for Intel processors, it also has led to a shortage of memory chips — a type of semiconductor made by Samsung Electronics Co, SK Hynix Inc and Micron Technology Inc. That, in turn, has forced up the price of laptops and desktops, and reduced demand for the Intel chips that go into those products.

Intel’s foundry unit had sales of US$6.7 billion, an increase of 58% from the period a year earlier. That business is trying to compete in a market dominated by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. The hope is to win enough outside customers to offset the massive cost of building chip factories and make Intel’s facilities more profitable.

Intel’s third-quarter gross margin, the percentage of revenue remaining after deducting the cost of production, was 43%. That benchmark shows the health of a company’s chipmaking operations in a costly and competitive industry. Intel projected the margin will narrow to 38% in the current period.

Though Intel now has enough of a financial cushion to weather downturns, such as the current PC market slump, it still needs to invest in its technology to stay competitive in the long run. It has lost market share to Advanced Micro Devices Inc in PC and server chips while also struggling to crack the lucrative AI accelerator category dominated by Nvidia.

stories.title: Amazon taps US$80 bil supplier loan facility to help fund AI
stories.summary: Amazon.com Inc has set up supplier financing arrangements to borrow as much as US$80 billion (RM325 billion) against the value of hardware it buys, the company’s latest move to preserve financial flexibility as it spends hundreds of billions on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Amazon动用800亿美元供应商贷款工具为AI提供资金
stories.content:
(Oct 31): Amazon.com Inc has set up supplier financing arrangements to borrow as much as US$80 billion (RM325 billion) against the value of hardware it buys, the company’s latest move to preserve financial flexibility as it spends hundreds of billions on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

Amazon has so far funded data centre construction and purchases of chips with the cash from its cloud-computing and retail operations, and with its biggest-ever corporate bond sales.

But it had largely avoided the sort of creative funding arrangements used by some of its rivals, including deals with investment groups to jointly finance data centre construction or to lease chips purchased by other entities. Many of those deals have focused on the Nvidia Corp chips that power most AI work and are often the single most expensive component of new data centre construction.

The secured loan facility, which Amazon disclosed in a quarterly filing after reporting earnings on Thursday, can be tapped at the company’s discretion from the beginning of 2027 through the third quarter of 2028. Lenders will get collateral rights over some of the assets purchased in connection with the facility. Amazon’s filing doesn’t specify what those assets included, and a spokesperson declined to comment.

“When we see such a really large opportunity in front of us, we are looking for ways to also responsibly fund that so that we can go as big as possible for our customers,” Amazon Web Services chief executive officer Matt Garman said in an interview on Bloomberg Television on Friday. Amazon, he said, was working with partners to “figure out how we can balance some of those cash flows as we’re really ramping up aggressively”.

On Thursday, Amazon reported a larger-than-expected increase in capital spending in its third-quarter earnings. The outlays led to a free cash outflow of US$42.4 billion during the year ended Sept 30. The shares were down about 2% at midday in New York.

Amazon’s total spending commitments — including debt and interest, leases not yet commenced, obligations to acquire property and equipment and other line items — ballooned to US$883 billion at the end of September, up 36% from three months earlier and more than double where that figure stood at the same point in 2025.

stories.title: The AI frenzy gets a reality check
stories.summary: Markets are starting to ask whether AI revenue can justify a trillion-dollar build-out
stories.title_zh: AI狂热遭遇现实检验
stories.content:
Markets are starting to ask whether AI revenue can justify a trillion-dollar build-out

THE initial euphoria over artificial intelligence has hit a speed bump. For the past three years, the market has treated every dollar spent on AI as a downpayment on the future. But over the past month, it has started asking some hard questions.

Shares in the hyperscalers – Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta – have fallen, and the selling has spread to the chipmakers and cloud providers that supply them.

The S&P 500, which is heavily weighted towards the hyperscalers and chipmaker Nvidia, is barely above its August peak. In the month to Oct 23, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was down 14 per cent. The biggest listed specialist AI cloud provider, CoreWeave, has lost more than 38 per cent.

Meanwhile, Treasury bonds, the classic safe haven for investors, have rallied despite rising inflation, which normally leads them to fall.

No single piece of bad news explains this performance. Rather, investors appear to be confronting a question that the euphoria had made them defer: Can the revenue from AI ever catch up with the spending?

The sums involved are staggering. The four big hyperscalers alone are on course to spend roughly US$700 billion on capital expenditure in 2026 and close to US$1 trillion in 2027, most of it on data centres and the chips that fill them.

## Lessons from past manias

In sheer scale, the AI build-out invites comparison with the great infrastructure booms of the past: the railway manias of Victorian Britain and Gilded Age America, and the fibre-optic and dot-com frenzies of the late 1990s.

Those precedents were premised on the notion that transformative technologies justify heavy spending. They are better read as a warning. Each was a vast bet on future demand, and each ended in a bust.

Britain’s railway mania collapsed in 1847, wiping out thousands of investors. In America, overbuilt lines helped trigger the panics of the late 19th century. Telecommunications carriers poured roughly US$500 billion into networks in the late 1990s, and by 2002 the Nasdaq had lost almost 80 per cent of its value.

In every case, the infrastructure went on to transform the economy, but the early investors who paid for it mostly did not share in the gains.

Each boom overestimated how quickly demand would grow. The problem was not the technology but the timing.

By 2001, only a small, single-digit fraction of the fibre laid in America was actually operational. The network eventually filled up – it carries today’s internet traffic – but not before one-time telecom giants WorldCom, Global Crossing and dozens of others had collapsed.

The same mismatch is visible now. Data centre construction is following an exponential curve, with each year’s plans dwarfing the last.

But AI adoption is not exponential. It seems to advance in fits and starts: first, there is a burst of enthusiasm; then, a long plateau as organisations work out how to reorganise around deploying a new tool; and then, maybe another leap.

A widely cited Massachusetts Institute of Technology study in July 2025 found that 95 per cent of organisations saw no measurable positive return on investment after six months. It is organisations, not individuals, that will drive most AI revenue.

## The revenue gap

No hyperscaler is likely to be making money on generative AI. Microsoft and Amazon, the only two to disclose AI revenue, report a combined annualised revenue of US$60 billion to US$70 billion – against around US$400 billion in capital spending between them in 2026 alone.

By some estimates, covering current and planned AI capex through identifiable AI income would require something like US$2.5 trillion a year – more than the combined revenue of the entire technology sector today.

Meanwhile, valuations across much of the AI ecosystem have run far ahead of earnings. Today’s share prices make sense only if AI delivers productivity gains far larger than anything yet visible in the data. That doesn’t mean the bet is wrong.

But investors are paying now for a transformation that may arrive much later, and patience is finite. Markets need not conclude that AI is a failure to reprice it sharply. They need only decide that the payoff is further off than they had assumed.

## Money that goes in circles

What further complicates the story is the way the industry finances itself. A growing share of AI demand rests on recycled capital, vendor financing and promises of future purchases.

For example, Nvidia has invested US$30 billion in OpenAI, which will in turn fill its data centres with Nvidia chips and has guaranteed up to US$105 billion in leases on a data centre campus that will host its chips for OpenAI. Nvidia holds a stake in CoreWeave, a cloud provider that buys its chips, and has agreed to purchase capacity that CoreWeave cannot sell.

Oracle has booked a contract worth around US$300 billion to supply computing power to OpenAI, a company still losing billions of dollars a year.

In such arrangements, one company’s capital expenditure becomes another’s revenue. Reported growth can stay spectacular without proving that the ecosystem has a self-sustaining economic model. When suppliers fund customers who then buy from those same suppliers, separating genuine demand from financial engineering becomes difficult.

The question is not whether demand exists – it does. The question is whether it will eventually generate enough revenue from customers outside the AI ecosystem – the banks, retailers, hospitals and manufacturers that must ultimately pay the bills – to justify the capital already committed.

## Borrowing against the future

Debt adds another layer of risk. Since 2025, bond issuance has funded a rising share of AI capital spending, as even the cash-rich hyperscalers have turned to credit markets to raise money.

Hyperscaler bond issuance soared from around US$17 billion in 2024 to US$109 billion in 2025 and US$194 billion in the first half of 2026.

Meta raised US$30 billion in a single bond sale and arranged a further US$27 billion for its Hyperion data centre in Louisiana through an off-balance-sheet vehicle with private credit provider Blue Owl Capital. Oracle, more stretched than its peers, has borrowed heavily to meet its OpenAI commitments.

Credit markets have noticed. Trading in credit default swaps (CDS) on hyperscalers and their suppliers, which insure against defaults, has surged, with Oracle’s spreads serving as the bellwether of what traders now call the AI hyperscaler default trade.

The volumes of CDS linked to seven AI-linked companies traded more than US$9 billion a week in September, up more than fourfold from the US$2 billion weekly average in July.

What worries these investors is not an outright collapse. The problem is that debt has been raised against forecasts that assume AI spending will keep accelerating, while interest and lease payments are fixed. The real test of resilience, then, is not whether the cycle can survive a collapse in spending, but whether it can survive spending that merely stops accelerating.

## Chips with a short shelf life

There is reason to think this cycle could be harsher on investors than its predecessors. Railway track and fibre-optic cable stayed productive for decades; later investors who bought bankrupt networks for cents on the dollar did very well out of them.

Graphics processing units (GPUs) – the chips that power AI – offer no such consolation. New chips outperform older ones so quickly that a GPU may pay its way for only two to five years. And if data centre construction is delayed, the chips that firms buy may have to remain in storage and run the risk of becoming obsolete.

Data Center Watch counts roughly US$200 billion worth of projects blocked or delayed by local opposition in the first half of 2026 alone.

Projects have also been held back by power and building shortages. Microsoft’s CEO, Satya Nadella, warned as early as November 2025 that the company might end up with “a bunch of chips sitting in inventory that I can’t plug in”.

None of this means AI is a mirage. It will almost certainly transform economies, productivity and work over the coming decades, as the railways and the internet did before it. But current valuations and investment levels assume that transformation will happen faster, and more profitably, than the evidence supports.

The web of cross-shareholdings and circular financing leaves the industry exposed to any loss of confidence, anywhere in the chain. When reality falls short of inflated expectations, as it usually does, a painful correction looks likely. The past month may prove to be only the first instalment. THE STRAITS TIMES

stories.title: AI deployments reshape colocation trust, transparency needs
stories.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) workloads are altering traditional colocation requirements, moving beyond facility uptime to demand high-density power and liquid cooling. This shift necessitates greater transparency and standardised resilience definitions from operators.
stories.title_zh: AI部署重塑colocation信任与透明度需求
stories.content:
The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) deployments is fundamentally changing the requirements for colocation data centres, according to a Schneider Electric blog post. Historically, colocation focused on providing reliable facilities with clear service level agreements (SLAs) for uptime, power, and security.AI workloads, however, span complex infrastructures including power systems, liquid cooling, high-performance networking, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), and software platforms. This complexity means facility uptime alone no longer guarantees workload success, creating a trust gap between providers and customers.
### Evolving Infrastructure for AI

AI-ready colocation facilities must support engineering requirements such as rack densities up to 227kW, direct-to-chip (DTC) liquid cooling, and readiness for transient power behaviour. Beyond physical infrastructure, operators and customers need a shared understanding of how this infrastructure will be monitored and managed.Effective AI operations require enhanced infrastructure visibility, with shared data on power utilisation, cooling performance, environmental conditions, and asset health. Traditional monitoring systems for facility and IT were often separate, creating blind spots that AI infrastructure cannot tolerate.
### New SLA and Resilience Standards

Traditional colocation SLAs, focused on facility availability, are insufficient for AI workloads. New SLAs must address power stability, thermal anomaly detection, remediation timelines, and escalation ownership, measuring performance relevant to AI operations.The absence of standardised resilience assumptions (N+1, concurrently maintainable, fault-tolerant) is a significant challenge in AI colocation. Differing interpretations of these terms can erode trust, necessitating clear, standardised definitions across all stakeholders.
### Shared Responsibility and Competitive Edge

The future of AI colocation will involve explicit shared responsibility frameworks, clearly defining domains for providers, customers, and jointly managed areas like monitoring and compliance. This approach reduces operational friction and builds customer confidence.Colocation providers that establish standardised frameworks for visibility, SLA reporting, resilience, and shared responsibilities will gain a competitive advantage. Customers expect predictable outcomes and transparent operations as AI deployments scale.

- Operations & Resilience
- 2 min Read

# AI deployments reshape colocation trust, transparency needs

Artificial intelligence (AI) workloads are altering traditional colocation requirements, moving beyond facility uptime to demand high-density power and liquid cooling. This shift necessitates greater transparency and standardised resilience definitions from operators.

stories.title: Power shortages leave AI chips idle in data centres
stories.summary: Billions of dollars worth of installed AI GPUs remain idle in data centres globally due to insufficient electrical supply to power and cool the chips, creating what industry observers term "dark GPU" capacity. The gap between semiconductor procurement and power infrastructure delivery is widening as AI investment cycles outpace utility grid expansion and substation commissioning timelines.
stories.why_it_matters: Dark GPUs represent stranded capital that inflates effective AI compute costs and threatens return on investment for data centre operators, while signaling to utilities and regulators that grid interconnection queues have become a binding constraint on national AI competitiveness that demands policy intervention.
stories.title_zh: 电力短缺导致AI芯片在数据中心闲置
stories.summary_zh: 全球数据中心中价值数十亿美元已安装的 AI GPU 因电力供应不足无法供电和冷却而保持闲置，形成了行业观察者所称的 "dark GPU" capacity。随着 AI 投资周期超过电网扩张和变电站投运时间线，半导体采购与电力基础设施交付之间的差距正在扩大。
stories.why_zh: Dark GPU 代表了抬高有效 AI 计算成本并威胁数据中心运营商投资回报的 stranded capital，同时向 utility 和监管机构发出信号：电网互联排队已成为制约国家 AI 竞争力的 binding constraint，需要政策干预。
stories.content:
Power shortages are leaving billions of dollars' worth of artificial intelligence (AI) chips unused at data centres, Business Insider reported. These idle chips, known as "dark GPUs," point to a widening gap between AI infrastructure investment and available power.Amazon Web Services (AWS) expects to receive about $5 billion worth of Nvidia GB300 server racks in August this year, followed by around $3 billion worth every month, Business Insider reported. Some of this equipment is being stored in warehouses until the necessary power infrastructure becomes available.Dark GPUs refer to purchased but unused graphics processing units (GPUs) that cannot be switched on or fully utilised. This can be due to inadequate electricity supply, incomplete data centre infrastructure, or system design issues, according to the report.Building a data centre and securing the required electricity supply can take years. Grid connections, transmission infrastructure, and approvals can delay projects even after hardware purchases.Epoch AI estimated in December 2025 that GPUs account for about 40 per cent of the electricity used by frontier AI data centres at peak operation. Cooling, networking, and other infrastructure consume much of the remaining power.Idle GPUs tie up billions of dollars in investment, as they do not immediately generate revenue. Companies also incur costs for storing, maintaining, and installing the equipment.The problem creates financial pressure and can delay the deployment of AI services and cloud computing capacity for developers. Morgan Stanley reported in October that US data centre developers faced an estimated net power shortfall of 34 per cent through 2028.Amazon plans to spend $220 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, with CEO Andy Jassy expecting even more in 2027. The company's free cash flow turned negative by $42.4 billion over the trailing 12 months, primarily due to higher spending on property and equipment driven by AI investments.

- AI & Compute Infrastructure
- 2 min Read

stories.title: Synergy: Enterprise cloud infrastructure spending jumped 55% YoY in Q3
stories.summary: The 12th consecutive quarter of growth
stories.title_zh: Synergy：第三季度企业云基础设施支出同比增长55%
stories.content:
Enterprise spending on cloud infrastructure services in Q3 jumped 55 percent year-over-year, the 12th consecutive quarter of growth, according to Synergy Research Group.

Synergy’s latest cloud market growth data revealed that global cloud revenue reached $168 billion in Q3 2026, more than double the revenue in the same period in 2024.

Growth was seen in all regions globally. The largest market remains the US, at 44 percent market share; it also has the highest growth rate among major countries.

According to Synergy, cloud market growth had been declining before the launch of ChatGPT in 2022. AI has driven year-on-year growth rates, with 185 percent growth since 2022. As of Q3 2026, AI-specific cloud services represent a third of the total market.

“AI has totally transformed the cloud market in terms of service capabilities, customer demand, and growth opportunities,” said John Dinsdale, chief analyst at Synergy Research Group.

“In the ten years before the launch of ChatGPT, cloud providers drove a rapid shift in workloads and investment from on-premises data centers towards public cloud services. What we now see is AI technology propelling cloud markets in a way that was unimaginable just four years ago. As the growth rate jumps to well over 50 percent, the leading cloud providers are benefiting from surging revenues, but they are also facing a much-changed market landscape, with AI labs and neoclouds emerging as both partners and competitors.”

Synergy’s data also reveals the breakdown of the major cloud providers, with Amazon taking the lead in the market, at 26 percent market share. The providers with the next two highest market shares are Microsoft (19 percent) and Google (16 percent). Both are improving their growth rates.

According to the data, neoclouds continue to erode the market share of the top cloud providers.

stories.title: Intel says Israel fab explosion will cost company $600m in losses, as Q3 '26 revenue hits $16.5bn

The company noted that operating losses at its Intel Foundry division narrowed quarter-over-quarter and anticipates announcing customers for its advanced 14A process node in the near future.
stories.why_it_matters: The Israel facility damage tightens advanced semiconductor supply at a moment when AI demand is already straining fabrication capacity, while Intel's reliance on 14A customer announcements to sustain investor confidence highlights the precariousness of its foundry turnaround strategy against entrenched competitors TSMC and Samsung.
stories.title_zh: Intel表示以色列晶圆厂爆炸将导致公司损失6亿美元，Q3 '26收入达165亿美元
stories.summary_zh: Intel 披露其以色列 fabrication 设施发生的爆炸将导致约 6 亿美元的损失，同时报告 2026 年第三季度收入为 165 亿美元。该公司指出其 Intel Foundry 部门的运营亏损环比收窄，并预计很快将宣布其先进 14A process node 的客户。
stories.why_zh: 以色列设施损坏在 AI 需求已使 fabrication capacity 紧张的关头收紧了先进半导体供应，而 Intel 依赖 14A 客户公告来维持投资者信心，凸显了其 foundry 转型策略在面对根深蒂固的竞争对手 TSMC 和 Samsung 时的脆弱性。
stories.content:
The explosion at Intel’s Kiryat Gat chip fabrication facility in Israel earlier this month will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue across two quarters, the company said during its Q3 2026 earnings call.

Describing the incident as an “unfortunate and tragic accident,” Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan told analysts that the incident led to a two-week shutdown of the factory, which will impact the chipmaker’s Q4 10-nanometer server shipments.

Two workers were killed, and another was seriously injured following an explosion at Intel’s Kiryat Gat chip fab earlier this month. According to local media reports at the time, police suspect the explosion resulted from a gas cylinder malfunctioning whilst it was being unloaded from a truck, with Israel’s Fire and Rescue Services stating that following the blast, a nitrogen trifluoride (NF3) leak occurred.

Nitrogen trifluoride is a toxic gas primarily used in semiconductor manufacturing for cleaning and etching silicon wafers. NF3 is non-flammable but can be highly dangerous if inhaled.

On the earnings call, Intel’s CFO, David Zinsner, said that the company was hoping to restart production at the site “by the end of this week,” and had been assessing wafers to see what is usable and what would need to be scrapped.

“This is somewhat of an early assessment, both really of Q4 \[2026\] and of Q1 \[2027\], but I think the current thinking is that we will have about a $300 million impact to the fourth quarter. That is likely to be similar in the first quarter,” he noted.

## Intel revenues up

Intel reported third-quarter revenue of $16.5 billion, up 21 percent Year-over-Year (YoY), with data center and AI (DCAI) revenue up 17 percent Quarter-over-Quarter (QoQ) and 78 percent YoY to $7.3 billion, with growth seen across hyperscale, enterprise, and neocloud customers.

“We also continued to see strong momentum in purpose-built silicon, with revenue increasing more than 50 percent sequentially and more than doubling YoY,” Zinsner said. However, despite Intel’s efforts to increase capacity, he said that demand for DCAI products continued to exceed available supply.

“DCAI operating profit was $3 billion, representing 42 percent of revenue and increasing approximately $600 million sequentially,” he added. “The improvement was driven by higher revenue and lower operating expenses. Granite Rapids is now the largest product family in our server portfolio as we continue to increase output from our Ireland facility.“

Meanwhile, Intel Foundry revenue was up 16 percent QoQ to $6.7bn, which Zinsner attributed to “better-than-expected growth on Intel 3 and Intel 18A.” External foundry revenue totaled $411 million for the three-month period – a sequential increase of $118m – with the unit reporting an operating loss of $1.9 billion, down from $2.1bn in Q2 2026.

“During the quarter, Intel 3 and Intel 18A yields both increased again, with Intel 18A improving at a double-digit rate,” Tan said on the earnings call. “Wafer output on both nodes exceeded expectations. Intel 18A-P remains on track for launch by year-end across our internal product portfolio, and external customer engagement continues to build.”

He added that the chipmaker was engaged with “a couple of highly strategic customers,” and he remained "increasingly confident that our Intel 18A-P will be an attractive node for external foundry customers."

With regard to Intel's 14A process node, which Tan has previously said the company would only move forward with if a "meaningful external customer to drive acceptable returns on our deployed capital” could be found, the CEO told analysts he was “highly encouraged by the progress we are making with multiple potential customers on 14A.”

In April of this year, Tesla CEO Elon Musk said that the EV company was planning to use Intel’s 14A chip manufacturing process at its $20 billion ‘TeraFab’ project in Austin, Texas. While Tan did not name the customers on the call, he said Intel would be ready to announce “a couple” in the next two quarters.

The quarter wasn’t entirely positive for Intel, however. Falling YoY revenue in the company’s client computing and physical AI group, combined with a weak fourth-quarter revenue forecast, saw Intel’s shares fall by around 20 percent in extended trading.

“We're guiding Q4 revenue to a range of $15-$16 billion,” Zinsner told analysts.

The CFO said that despite the anticipated financial impact of the explosion, Intel still expects 2027 to be a “growth year” and is expecting the momentum its DCAI segment experienced during Q3 to continue into the fourth quarter and beyond.

“The only little nuance is the first half of the year; we are still a bit constrained. We talked about putting 40 percent more capacity in substrates, but a lot of that does not hit us until the back half of the year,” he said.

In an effort to address these pressures, Zinsner said Tan had been in Japan talking to substrate vendors to make sure Intel continued to receive its “allocated and appropriate supply.”

“I think we are as well positioned as anyone out there in terms of delivering supply. It is tight. It is going to be tight this next quarter and going into the first half \[of 2027\]. But I think we positioned ourselves well so that beyond that, we should start to see some pretty healthy growth in the data center business.”

stories.title: The network wall: why switches aren't scaling fast enough for AI data centers
stories.summary: A failure to scale could hurt data center operators
stories.title_zh: 网络墙：为什么交换机对于AI数据中心的扩展速度不够快
stories.content:
The scale of AI data centers is typically described in terms of three resources: cost, number of GPUs (i.e., cluster size), and the amount of power required. That's because those resources are key constraints that determine how much AI processing a data center will be able to perform.

But there’s another constraint that has quietly become just as critical: the back-end network that connects GPUs. The network, together with power, increasingly determines not only how many accelerators (GPUs, XPUs and other processors used for AI workloads) can be deployed in a data center, but also how efficiently and productively they can be used. Network architecture can also significantly affect how complicated the facility is to build and operate, how rapidly it can be brought online and therefore how quickly it can begin generating revenue.

A network that struggles to keep pace with the demands of AI creates a hard limit on the scale and productivity of the infrastructure that can be built — what is often referred to as the network wall. For that reason, the network needs to be a primary design consideration when building and operating AI data centers.

## The critical role of the network

The network has a direct impact on not only the design parameters of an AI data center — density, power, cost — but also on the key metrics that drive the productivity and success of the data center. The impact is so significant that a hyperscaler I spoke with recently stated that they start with the network and design their data center buildings based on what the network can support.

AI processing relies on rapidly exchanging large amounts of data among accelerators synchronously and repeatedly — gradients, context, KV caches, and attention tensors are just a few examples of the data that accelerators need to exchange in coordinated operations, known as collective communication, during AI processing.

Collectives such as All-to-All require every GPU across a cluster to exchange data with every other GPU, while operations such as All-Reduce and All-Gather depend on data from every other GPU in the cluster. Because these collectives are synchronized operations, all participating GPUs need to wait for all data to arrive before moving on to the next step in processing.

The design and capabilities of the network have a critical impact on the performance of those operations. Network architecture decisions, topology, partitioning, oversubscription ratio, number of rails and planes, as well as technology choices such as interconnect technology, switch bandwidth and switch radix (the number of ports that can connect to a single non-blocking switch chip) determine the speed of communication among GPUs. As a result, network congestion and latency degrade the performance of AI processing.

In addition to performance, the network infrastructure also impacts cost, complexity and reliability. Network design and technology determine the total number of switches, switching tiers, fibers, and optical transceivers required to create the network fabric connecting accelerators. That, in turn, impacts the number of network racks that need to be powered and cooled, the number of components that can fail, and the share of the overall budget that needs to go to the network.

Those impacts ultimately drive the performance, efficiency, and scalability that determine the productivity and competitive advantage that an AI data center delivers for training and inference. Whether for an AI lab racing to develop the best model or for a neocloud competing to deliver the best inference performance for AI applications, those metrics are critical to success.

One example: tokens per second, a measure of AI processing throughput, suffers when GPUs are forced to sit idle and underutilized because they are waiting for data movement across the network. In fact, the network is a major reason that GPUs in AI clusters can spend a large share of their time idle and underutilized, often below 50 percent in published production traces. Poor GPU utilization increases the time it takes to train models and the rate at which inference requests can be served.

Tokens per watt, an increasingly important efficiency metric due to the challenges of securing the power necessary for AI data centers, is also directly impacted by the network. Underutilized GPUs still consume significant amounts of power, even while waiting for data. Adding network tiers, switches, and optics to support larger and larger AI data centers increases the power consumed by network switches and optics, further reducing tokens per watt.

Tokens per dollar is also directly influenced by the network. Both the direct cost of the network — switches, optics, cables, etc. — and the indirect cost of underutilized GPUs contribute to the cost efficiency of an AI data center. Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, highlighted that significance in his keynote address at the GTC conference in Washington, D.C., when he noted that for a 1GW data center, which costs on the order of $50 billion to build, a ten percent change in GPU utilization has an economic impact of $5bn, while SemiAnalysis indicates that the network is often the second-largest cost in an AI cluster after the accelerators themselves.

Finally, the network contributes to the complexity of the data center, which impacts time to value. Every additional switch and fiber must be procured, installed, inspected, tested, configured, and monitored. More components create more opportunities for a failed optic, contaminated connector, cabling error, or underperforming link to delay completion. Taken together, that complexity can directly add to the time to bring a new data center into operation. Because of financing and lease obligations, as well as the approach of new generations of GPUs, those delays matter: a recent Carnegie Endowment financial model estimated that a one-year delay reduces the lifecycle value of an illustrative 100MW US data center by roughly $550 million, or 5.5 percent.

## The growing pressure on the network

Despite how critical they are to the data center, AI networks are under increasing strain and struggling to keep up, not only because demand for AI training and inference is necessitating ever-larger clusters and data centers, but also because AI algorithms and architectures are evolving and advancing along several dimensions at once.

GPU performance has continued to race ahead with each new generation, able to consume and generate tokens and data at higher and higher rates. For example, Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra GPU delivers roughly a 2.5x increase in compute performance over the Hopper-generation H200 that came to market only a year before.

The evolution of AI models is adding additional demands on the network. Mixture-of-experts models require rapidly routing data among different experts. Longer model context windows and multimodal processing increase the size of the data set that needs to be distributed for models to process. Disaggregating prefill and decode steps in inference processing creates new data movement demands between GPUs and other accelerators. Agentic AI workloads, often orchestrated by a separate CPU rack, can trigger hundreds of concurrent API calls for inference processing during their work.

The network is falling further and further behind. Network switch bandwidth and radix have been increasing at a much slower pace, with the just-emerging 102.4T generation of switches coming to market almost four years after the previous-generation 51.2T switches, continuing a historical pace of doubling only every two to four years.

When bandwidth and radix per switch are insufficient, the network design is forced to expand to compensate. Additional switches and network tiers are added, which in turn require more inter-switch connections, more optical transceivers, and more cabling. Not only does that add more cost, power, and complexity; it also increases latency and congestion, leading to underperforming networks that reduce GPU utilization and slow down AI training and inference.

## Breaking through the network wall

The network can no longer be an afterthought, considered only after determining GPUs, racks, power, and cooling architecture. By the time a bottleneck becomes visible in production, the opportunity to fix it without massive disruption has already closed. Networking architecture and technology need to be part of data center design from early stages.

Flatter networks with fewer tiers, fewer switches, fewer inter-switch links, fewer optics and cables, lower power, faster commissioning, and more predictable workload performance are crucial goals that need to be part of the design. Achieving those goals requires network switches with significantly higher radix *and* bandwidth to keep up with the pace of computational throughput, bandwidth per GPU, larger clusters, and new AI algorithms and architectures that demand more data movement. High-radix switch platforms can deliver that while simplifying the network. That not only prevents delays in bringing a new data center online, but also improves the throughput and resulting economic impact of the entire data center over its lifetime.

The gap between architectural ambition and network reality is where competitive position will be decided. Treating networking as a critical part of data center design and embracing high-radix switching will provide a crucial advantage to the winners of this race.

stories.title: Alibaba Cloud goes live in Amsterdam as European expansion continues
stories.summary: Alibaba Cloud, a global provider of artificial intelligence infrastructure and the intelligence backbone of Alibaba Group, announced the launch of its first public cloud region in Amsterdam, Netherlands, with two new data centers available to meet demand for cloud and AI services in Europe. Alibaba Cloud said in a press release that the new region […]
stories.title_zh: Alibaba Cloud阿姆斯特丹上线，欧洲扩张继续
stories.content:
Alibaba Cloud, a global provider of artificial intelligence infrastructure and the intelligence backbone of Alibaba Group, announced the launch of its first public cloud region in Amsterdam, Netherlands, with two new data centers available to meet demand for cloud and AI services in Europe.

Alibaba Cloud said in a press release that the new region offers a comprehensive suite of cloud computing products including elastic computing, storage, container, networking, big data, security, database, and cloud-native services. The company also plans to bring a suite of agentic AI services to the region.

“The Netherlands is one of Europe’s most vibrant digital economies, and our first region here is a direct response to the strong demand we see from local businesses building and scaling with AI. By bringing our advanced AI and cloud capabilities to Amsterdam, we are giving customers the in-region infrastructure, performance and data residency they need to innovate faster, scale securely and operate with greater efficiency in the AI era,” said Feifei Li, Alibaba Cloud Intelligence President of International Business and Chief Technology Officer.

In August, Alibaba Cloud launched its first cloud region in Brazil. Like the Netherlands, the Brazil region launched with a suite of products, and agentic AI services are in the offing. The launch of these cloud regions is part of Alibaba’s US$ 53 billion investment in AI and cloud infrastructure globally.

The Netherlands is the fourth Alibaba Cloud region to come online in Europe joining Frankfurt in Germany, London in the UK and Paris in France. The launch grows the company’s availability zones to 109 across 32 regions worldwide. Alibaba Cloud also plans to launch its first cloud region in Finland, while the company looks to expand its data center footprint in Germany and France over the next 12 months.

According to MarketsandMarkets, the cloud computing market in the Netherlands is expected to grow from a value of US$ 14.6 billion in 2025 to US$ 27.5 billion by 2030. This growth is being fueled by increasing demand for data analytics, AI integration, and hybrid cloud solutions. The country’s robust data center ecosystem and compliance with European data protection standards position it as a critical cloud services hub.

stories.title: Nuclear potential, data centre boom may be addressed in new Asean energy masterplan
stories.summary: ASEAN member states may incorporate nuclear energy and data centre growth scenarios into a revised regional energy masterplan currently under development. Industry participants emphasize that realizing this potential requires harmonized regulatory frameworks for cross-border power trading through ASEAN Power Grid initiatives, where progress has lagged technical feasibility studies.
stories.why_it_matters: Explicit inclusion of data centre demand in regional energy planning would elevate digital infrastructure from an afterthought to a core planning variable, but the persistent gap between ASEAN Power Grid ambition and implementation means Southeast Asian data centre operators likely face continued patchwork national regulations rather than seamless regional energy markets for years to come.
stories.title_zh: Nuclear potential, data centre boom may be addressed in new ASEAN energy masterplan
stories.summary_zh: 东盟成员国可能将核能和数据中心增长情景纳入目前正在修订的区域能源 masterplan。行业参与者强调，实现这一潜力需要通过 ASEAN Power Grid initiative 进行跨境电力交易的协调监管框架，而该领域的进展一直落后于技术可行性研究。
stories.why_zh: 将数据中心需求明确纳入区域能源规划将数字基础设施从事后考虑提升为核心规划变量，但 ASEAN Power Grid 雄心与实施之间的持续差距意味着，东南亚数据中心运营商在未来数年内可能继续面临拼凑的国家法规，而非无缝的区域能源市场。
stories.content:
But Asean Power Grid projects need rules to be in place to deliver on potential, say industry players

\[SINGAPORE\] An upcoming masterplan for the Asean Power Grid (APG) could take into account room for nuclear energy in the region, alongside other emerging forms of clean power, said Razib Dawood, executive director of the Asean Centre for Energy (ACE). The growing energy demand from a boom in data centres could also feature in the outlook.

The centre has just started work on the fourth edition of the Asean Interconnection Masterplan Study (AIMS), which explores the viability of cross-border electricity trade in the region, Razib told *The Business Times*. The study is likely to be completed in about a year.

He noted that there have been significant changes in the energy landscape since ACE and the head of the Asean Power Utilities/Authorities Council released the previous edition of AIMS in 2024.

That report made no mention of data centres, but these facilities have since mushroomed across Asean and become a major guzzler of electricity.

In October, ACE projected that data centres would account for 20.7 per cent of the region’s electricity demand growth between 2025 and 2030.

Earlier forecasts could not have expected that “suddenly they’d need gigawatts (of power) over a short period of time”, Razib said. He added that the ongoing AIMS review may also have to factor in Asean’s potential adoption of new technologies. These include pumped hydro storage, battery energy storage and small modular nuclear reactors in the longer run.

When asked, Razib said that it might eventually be possible for nuclear energy to be traded in the region as part of the APG, similar to how France exports nuclear energy to European neighbours such as Germany.

He is also bullish on the potential for increasing wind energy exports in the region, given the completion in 2025 of a successful project that exports wind power from Laos. Also, Singapore recently gave conditional approval for a project to import up to 1.3 gigawatts of renewable electricity from Vietnam and Malaysia, including wind-generated power.

## “Rules first” approach needed

That said, Razib acknowledged that “there may be some sceptics saying ‘you’ve been talking about this (APG) for over three decades... so why now?’”

But he believes that the time is right for the development of APG as the global energy crunch from conflict in the Middle East has renewed a drive for energy cooperation in South-east Asia. Against this backdrop, efforts to iron out APG policy details have continued.

For instance, Asean energy ministers in October endorsed the terms of reference for the Submarine Power Cables Development Framework. This will facilitate the laying, maintenance and protection of the undersea cables needed in the APG.

This comes as the industry has called for greater regulatory clarity on the ambitious regional interconnectivity project. Some APG interconnectors could require subsea cables to run more than 800 km – beating the world’s current record of 630 km.

Separately, Alessandro Panico, chief commercial officer and senior vice-president of the transmission business at Italian cable manufacturer Prysmian, urged a “rules first” approach to APG development.

In his view, the technical feasibility of laying long cables “will not really be a problem”, since existing technology theoretically allows maximum distances of more than 1,000 km.

Instead, “the bottleneck at the moment… is that the business case has to work”, he told BT. “Projects have to be bankable, and in order to do this, we need political willingness and regulatory frameworks.”

Prysmian has operated in Singapore for more than 50 years. It has a track record of supplying subsea cables for South-east Asian projects that deliver electricity to islands. This includes a subsea power cable system linking Phu Quoc to Vietnam’s national grid on the mainland.

The APG will step into new territory with cross-border undersea power linkages. While several grid connections already run overland between countries, South-east Asia now has only one cross-border subsea interconnector, running between Singapore and Johor.

While Panico sees potential for the APG to ramp up demand for subsea power cables, he stressed that political will is needed to realise these projects.

Still, regional electricity trade tends to bring down prices, he noted. There is “a lot of potential to create a proper Asean grid that will benefit, at the end of the day, all the taxpayers in the region”, he added.

stories.title: Edge AI inference offers telecoms a new growth engine
stories.summary: Edge AI inference could become a new growth engine for the telecommunications industry, potentially placing telcos closer to the center of AI infrastructure. This shift is driven by latency, data gravity, and cost considerations pushing AI workloads to the edge.
stories.title_zh: Edge AI inference为电信业提供新增长引擎
stories.content:
Edge AI inference is emerging as a new growth opportunity for the telecommunications industry, potentially positioning telcos closer to the core of AI inference infrastructure. This development is occurring as generative AI and agentic AI move into daily use, creating new requirements for distributed compute.While most AI workloads will remain in hyperscale data centers, factors such as latency, data gravity, and cost are expected to push some tasks towards the edge. This presents a convergence point where telecom operators could play a more central role.
### The Nuances of Edge AI Deployment

Nvidia has already indicated this opportunity, with projects and partnerships involving companies like AT&T, Charter Communications, Cisco, Nokia, SoftBank, Telefónica, and T-Mobile. Nvidia's focus includes edge AI for factory and robotics use cases, often termed “physical AI,” which is closely linked to AI-RAN.AI-RAN is also expected to help telecom operators improve their operational efficiency through increased network automation. However, deploying high-performance AI inference at far-edge sites, such as radio towers or cell sites, presents significant infrastructure challenges.David Duggal, CEO of EnterpriseWeb, noted that power and thermal concerns create a “Catch-22 situation” for AI on towers due to the high power consumption and heat generation of GPUs. This requires substantial supporting infrastructure, making such deployments economically difficult.The Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA) is working to define unified practices for AI data center infrastructure. Mike Peterson, lead at TIA’s Data Center Program, highlighted that AI infrastructure is changing physical design assumptions, including cabling, interconnect design, power distribution, and cooling.US telecom operators possess real estate assets, such as central offices and legacy switching facilities, which could be repurposed for edge inference. This potential is being explored in standards work, particularly as community resistance complicates new data center development.
### Latency vs. Workload Type

IDC’s senior research manager for cloud and data centers, Luis Fernandes, cautioned against overstating latency as the universal driver for pushing AI to the edge. Research by IDC and the European Commission found that while latency matters in specific cases, workload type is often a more determining factor.Real-time workloads necessitate instant responses shaped by local context, while analytical workloads typically do not. For enterprise buyers and operators, the key is to determine which workloads truly benefit from proximity to the point of action.Content delivery networks (CDNs) are naturally integrating into the edge AI landscape. Akamai is deploying GPU-equipped edge nodes within telecom central offices to orchestrate real-time traffic and distributed processing for applications like computer vision.Jon Alexander, senior vice president of products for Akamai’s Cloud Technology Group, stated that physical AI remains among the most latency-sensitive use cases. He added that metro-level edge infrastructure, delivering 5- to 10-millisecond response times, may suffice for a broad range of commercial AI workloads.

- AI & Compute Infrastructure
- 2 min Read

# Edge AI inference offers telecoms a new growth engine

Edge AI inference could become a new growth engine for the telecommunications industry, potentially placing telcos closer to the center of AI infrastructure. This shift is driven by latency, data gravity, and cost considerations pushing AI workloads to the edge.

- Published On Oct 30, 2026 at 05:30 PM IST

## Highlights

- Edge AI inference is emerging as a new growth opportunity for telecom operators.
- Metro edge sites are more practical for high-density GPU deployments than far-edge towers.
- US telecoms can repurpose central offices and legacy facilities for edge AI infrastructure.
- Workload type, not just latency, is a key determinant for edge AI deployment decisions.

stories.title: Japan's Marubeni looks to profit from bottlenecks arising from AI boom
stories.summary: Japanese trading house Marubeni is developing strategies to profit from infrastructure bottlenecks created by surging AI demand, including potential investments in power generation, data centre development, and semiconductor supply chain logistics. The company aims to leverage its existing energy and industrial project expertise to capture value from constraints that are delaying AI deployment across Asia-Pacific markets.
stories.why_it_matters: Marubeni's pivot toward bottleneck exploitation reflects a broader shift by diversified industrial conglomerates from commodity trading to infrastructure ownership, potentially accelerating power and logistics solutions for data centres while concentrating control over critical AI supply chain chokepoints in fewer hands.
stories.title_zh: 日本Marubeni寻求从AI热潮引发的瓶颈中获利
stories.summary_zh: 日本综合商社 Marubeni 正在制定从 AI 需求激增造成的基础设施瓶颈中获利的策略，包括潜在投资于发电、数据中心开发和半导体供应链物流。该公司旨在利用其现有的能源和工业项目专业知识，从阻碍亚太市场 AI 部署的约束中捕获价值。
stories.why_zh: Marubeni 向瓶颈利用的转向反映了多元化工业集团从商品贸易向基础设施所有权的更广泛转变，这可能加速数据中心的电力和物流解决方案，同时将关键 AI 供应链瓶颈的控制权集中在更少的手中。
stories.content:
Interview
# Japan's Marubeni looks to profit from bottlenecks arising from AI boom

CEO says energy, resource constraints can be source of growth for trading house

Marubeni, one of Japan's five big trading houses, sees physical constraints for energy and resources arising from the AI boom as an opportunity for growth. (Photo by Yuki Kohara)

SHOTARO TANI

October 30, 2026 11:25 JST

TOKYO -- Japanese trading house Marubeni is betting on physical bottlenecks such as demand for energy and natural resources stemming from the artificial intelligence boom to drive its growth, expanding its exposure to businesses that supply and manage the power, metals and communications infrastructure needed to support rising demand for computing power.

Documents show Queensland’s long-term energy plan is based on outdated assumptions that do not factor in any extra demand for electricity from data centres, even as Anthropic pushes ahead with one of the country’s largest facilities and the Crisafulli government vows fast-track approvals for others.

stories.title: Panasonic's battery unit posts higher 2Q operating profit, lifts forecast
stories.summary: TOKYO (Oct 30): Japan's Panasonic Holdings said on Friday that operating profit at its energy unit surged to 55.6 billion yen (US$352 million) in the second quarter from 1.2 billion yen a year earlier, boosted by higher sales of in-vehicle batteries and data centre energy storage systems.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Panasonic电池部门二季度营业利润增长，上调预测
stories.content:
TOKYO (Oct 30): Japan's Panasonic Holdings said on Friday that operating profit at its energy unit surged to 55.6 billion yen (US$352 million) in the second quarter from 1.2 billion yen a year earlier, boosted by higher sales of in-vehicle batteries and data centre energy storage systems.

Panasonic raised the unit's full-year profit forecast for the year ending March 2027 by 16% to 198 billion yen from 171 billion yen previously. The company makes batteries for Tesla and other EV makers.

It also lifted its group operating profit forecast for the period by 120 billion yen, or 20%, to 710 billion yen, in part due to stronger-than-expected growth in its AI-related businesses.

Panasonic said the unit's quarterly operating profit grew due to higher sales of EV batteries in North America and data centre energy storage systems.

It said demand from strategic customers for in-vehicle batteries continued to significantly outperform the overall market.

stories.content:
MEXICO CITY (Oct 29): Nvidia is in talks to offer AI cloud provider Nscale billions of dollars in credit guarantees to support debt funding for a data centre earmarked for Anthropic, *The Information* reported on Thursday, citing people with knowledge of the talks.

The credit support would help fund power infrastructure and construction of Nscale's AI data centre in West Virginia, which Anthropic plans to use, according to the report. Nvidia is an investor in the UK-based cloud provider.

The deal has not been signed and terms could still change, the report said.

Nvidia, Nscale and Anthropic did not immediately respond to *Reuters* requests for comment.

Claude maker Anthropic struck a deal in August to spend US$45 billion to rent computing power from Nscale's West Virginia data centre campus.

Nscale is also in talks to sell about 460 megawatts of AI computing power to Anthropic in another deal that could also be worth about US$45 billion.

The report comes as companies such as Coreweave and Firmus, which are both backed by Nvidia, have been hit by concerns about debt financing behind the AI build-out.

stories.title: NTT DATA grows AI Factory footprint to five sites
stories.summary: NTT DATA has expanded its AI Factory footprint to five global locations with new launches in Paris, Munich, and Singapore, joining existing facilities in Plano, Texas and Riyadh. The AI Factories provide integrated environments where enterprises can develop, train, and deploy AI models with access to specialized compute infrastructure and NTT's managed services expertise.
stories.why_it_matters: NTT DATA's rapid geographic expansion signals enterprise demand for sovereign and regional AI training capabilities that avoid data residency risks and latency penalties of centralized hyperscale clouds, while putting competitive pressure on local system integrators and telecom operators offering similar edge-AI services.
stories.title_zh: NTT DATA将AI Factory扩展至五个站点
stories.summary_zh: NTT DATA 已将其 AI Factory 足迹扩展至五个全球地点，新推出 Paris、Munich 和 Singapore 设施，加入现有位于 Plano, Texas 和 Riyadh 的设施。这些 AI Factory 提供集成环境，企业可在其中开发、训练和部署 AI 模型，并获得 specialized compute infrastructure 和 NTT 的托管服务专业知识。
stories.why_zh: NTT DATA 的快速地理扩张表明企业对主权和区域 AI 训练能力的需求，以避免集中式 hyperscale cloud 的数据驻留风险和延迟惩罚，同时对提供类似 edge-AI 服务的本地系统集成商和电信运营商施加竞争压力。
stories.content:
NTT DATA, an artificial intelligence, digital business, and technology services provider that forms part of NTT Group, has announced the global expansion of NTT DATA AI Factories, launching facilities in Paris, France, Munich, Germany, and Singapore this month to join existing AI factories in Plano, Texas, and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

These facilities help businesses and technology leaders evaluate AI workloads against real-world requirements including infrastructure architecture, performance workload placement, and cost. According to a press release, the AI factories are designed to help clients make deployment decisions with greater confidence and alleviate the bottlenecks stalling AI’s shift from pilot programs to production.

“AI at scale is ultimately about turning intelligence into measurable business impact,” said Dilip Kumar, NTT DATA President and Global Head, Infrastructure Solutions. “That requires organizations to balance innovation with responsibility and make informed choices about where AI creates value and how it can be deployed sustainably and economically. Our AI Factories help clients build that confidence before they scale.”

Earlier this month the company launched NTT DATA AI Factory Munich at the NTT Global Data Centers’ Munich 2 facility. The AI factory lets organizations test AI they make, own, and control against their own use cases before making investment decisions. The Munich 2 facility has 6,300 square meters of data center space across two buildings and a total critical IT load of 14 MW.

NTT DATA says that its AI Factories are underpinned by technology including Cisco Secure AI Factory with NVIDIA full-stack infrastructure built for neocloud and sovereign cloud demand. According to Cassie Roach, Cisco Global Vice President of AI Infrastructure and Connectivity Partner Sales, Cisco’s solution, combined with NTT DATA’s expanding presence, creates a strong foundation to transition AI workloads from experimentation into production.

“Scaling AI goes beyond computing. Enterprises need a secure and resilient infrastructure foundation that spans infrastructure, security, performance and operations — while maintaining control of their data and AI economics,” said Roach.

At the beginning of October, w.media reported that NTT DATA was nearing an agreement with Anthropic to develop a large-scale data center in Osaka, Japan, at a reported cost of US$ 6.3 billion. Neither firm has confirmed the deal, but negotiations are reportedly set to be completed by the end of March 2027. If the deal goes ahead, the facility would be Anthropic’s first dedicated data center in Japan. Partial operations could begin as soon as 2028.

stories.title_zh: NVIDIA CEO黄仁勋称与受间谍调查的新加坡公司关系"正常"
stories.content:
An executive of Megaspeed International is said to be under investigation for spying for China

\[SAN FRANCISCO\] Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang said the chipmaker’s dealings with Megaspeed International were “normal and not unusual” following a report by *The New York Times* that one of the Singapore firm’s executives is under investigation for spying on behalf of China.

Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed’s officials was proper, and the chipmaker has checked to ensure that Megaspeed did not illegally send its artificial intelligence processors to China, Huang said in an interview on Thursday (Oct 29).

That country is barred from buying Nvidia’s powerful AI chips – known as graphics processing units, or GPUs – under US export rules.

“We’ve studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one,” he said in the interview. “And I think the US government also has as well.”

The remarks follow a story by *The New York Times* that the US government is investigating an executive from Megaspeed for allegedly providing information to the Chinese government.

Huang Le has previously been pictured with Nvidia’s leader on social media, and the story reports that she may have been serving as a Chinese agent aiming to evade chip export controls.

In the interview, Huang said that his interactions with her were typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. She is no longer with Megaspeed, he said.

“Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual,” Huang said. The CEO said he had not been informed by the US government of its suspicions about Huang Le.

## Clampdowns on US tech exports

The growing geopolitical rivalry between the US and China has led to increasing clampdowns by Washington on exports of key American technology.

That has cut off Nvidia from a lucrative source of revenue in China, the largest market for chips.

The company has received some latitude to ship a limited amount of older AI-related products to the Asian country under the Trump administration.

That approval has not resulted in a material amount of shipments, at least in part because Beijing has sought to limit the deliveries itself in an effort to foster its own chip industry.

Nonetheless, the restrictions on exports have led to investigations and charges of smuggling of Nvidia’s best products to China – something the company has said is an insignificant issue.

Megaspeed is one of a group of companies that Bloomberg News and others have reported may have tried to illegally divert shipments of chips intended for data centres outside of China into that country. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Equinix posts record annualized gross bookings of $533m, up 35 percent
stories.summary: Equinix reported annualized gross bookings of US$533 million for its third quarter 2026, representing a 35 percent year-over-year increase that prompted the company to raise full-year guidance for the third consecutive quarter. The company projects fourth-quarter revenues between US$2.684 billion and US$2.724 billion, reflecting sustained demand across its global interconnection and colocation portfolio.
stories.why_it_matters: Consistently raised guidance in a capital-intensive sector signals that Equinix's premium pricing for interconnection services remains resilient despite competitive pressure from hyperscale cloud providers, validating the hybrid multi-cloud strategy that underpins enterprise demand for neutral colocation.
stories.title_zh: Equinix公布创纪录的年化总预订额5.33亿美元，同比增长35%
stories.summary_zh: Equinix 报告 2026 年第三季度 annualized gross bookings 为 5.33 亿美元，同比增长 35%，促使该公司连续第三个季度上调全年 guidance。该公司预计第四季度收入在 26.84 亿至 27.24 亿美元之间，反映其全球互联和 colocation 组合的持续需求。
stories.why_zh: 在资本密集型行业中持续上调 guidance 表明，尽管面临 hyperscale 云服务商的竞争压力，Equinix 对互联服务的 premium pricing 仍保持韧性，验证了支撑企业对 neutral colocation 需求的 hybrid multi-cloud 策略。
stories.content:
Colocation and interconnection giant Equinix posted revenues of $2.571 billion for the latest quarter, up 11 percent on the same time last year.

The company said that it delivered record annualized gross bookings of $533 million, up 35 percent. Equinix raised full-year 2026 guidance for the third consecutive quarter.

The company posted an operating income of $600 million, up 27 percent. Adjusted EBITDA was $1.321bn, up 15 percent.

"Our Q3 results and raised full-year guidance reflect the differentiated position and growing importance of Equinix," said Adaire Fox-Martin, CEO and president, Equinix.

"We delivered double-digit growth across the key metrics that drive long-term value creation, including interconnection and monthly recurring revenue, and we accelerated capacity to meet broad-based demand. We also unveiled Equinix Fabric One and Equinix Inference Exchange to enable enterprise customers to run, connect, and orchestrate their most critical workloads."

In an earnings call, Fox-Martin said that the company has "significantly increased" the number of cabinets it plans to deliver in the second half of this year, and expects to exceed its retail capacity plan for the full year by nearly 40 percent.

The company expects more than 13,000 cabinets in Q4, its highest quarter of delivery on record, with more than 20 percent of that Q4 capacity presold. 15 percent of retail capacity coming online in 2027 is presold.

"We have 3GW of developable capacity, which includes our projects currently in progress," she said.

"About 80 percent of that is in our top 25 metros, and the land, power and permitting is largely secured. On top of that 3GW, the atNorth transaction we completed this quarter with CPP Investments brings an active development pipeline of 800MW coming online over the next five years as well as an additional 1GW of opportunity for future expansion."

Without mentioning names, Fox-Martin appeared to differentiate Equinix's approach to that of large-scale neoclouds, which aim to develop giant facilities for large customer orders.

"Capacity isn't simply a numbers game," she said. "A megawatt in a major interconnection hub is worth more than one elsewhere."

She added: "We serve core critical workloads that run the everyday economy. Our new retail builds are sized for these use cases, generally 60MW or less, and they are substantially smaller than the large scale campuses drawing the most regulatory attention. We also don't depend on any single build to meet our growth objectives."

Similarly, no single client exceeds 2.5 percent of Equinix's total revenue. "The breadth of our customer base means that our results don't rely on any single customer, industry, geography or technology trend," she said.

CFO Olivier Leonetti said that customer churn was at 1.7 percent. "Customers churned out at an average density of 5kW per cabinet and in at an average density of 7kW per cabinet, reflecting rising densities from AI workloads."

Pricing on new deals was increased 12 percent year-over-year. "We expect this pricing strength will be durable," he said.

With this in mind, Fox-Martin admitted that "it is possible that we may choose to do selective churns where we may choose to churn out with intention a customer that's operating at a particular price point and perhaps low interconnection or network density and churn in a customer that has some of the opposite parameters."

Quarterly capex hit $1.6 billion, with roughly 90 percent directed towards capacity expansion.
